````math
### G.2 Signal Ablation

The second block of
Table [5](#S4.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 4.1 Main Results: PF Intervention, Selection, and Internalization ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ Harnessing LLM Agents with Skill Programs")
evaluates the contribution of each of the four supervision signals. All
rows in this block use the closed-loop rejection sampling experiment E5
(V2 RS,
§[D](#A4 "Appendix D Additional Experimental Details ‣ Harnessing LLM Agents with Skill Programs"))
and full filtering (Exec $`+`$ Teach), so the only knob that varies is
which subset of $`\{T,M,C,O\}`$ enters the per-step weight
$`A_{t}=\lambda_{t}t_{t}+\lambda_{m}m_{t}+\lambda_{q}q_{t}+\lambda_{o}o_{t}`$
used in
§[E](#A5 "Appendix E Fine-Grained Signal Composition ‣ Harnessing LLM Agents with Skill Programs").

All four signals. The default $`E5`$ run, with the canonical weights
$`(\lambda_{t},\lambda_{m},\lambda_{q},\lambda_{o})=(0.15,0.10,0.25,0.50)`$.
Reference row at $`60.3\%`$.

w/o Timing. The *timing* signal $`t_{t}`$ is dropped: the per-step score
no longer rewards firing on risky steps (FINAL with no read, FINAL at
low step count, SEARCH after empty results) or punishes firing on safe
ones. The remaining three signals are renormalized to sum to $`1`$. The
drop of $`-7.8`$ points indicates that, although timing carries the
smallest default weight, removing it lets the policy intervene at the
wrong steps and miss risky ones, both of which propagate into worse
downstream outcomes.

w/o Modality. The *modality* signal $`m_{t}`$ is dropped: the framework
no longer distinguishes MODIFY_ACTION (pre-action) from INJECT_CONTEXT
(post-observation) interventions. The drop of $`-15.5`$ points is the
largest, which we read as evidence that *how* an intervention fires
matters as much as *when*: rewriting a SEARCH query and injecting a
reading reminder are not interchangeable, and a model trained without
modality credit learns to treat them as such.

w/o Correctness. The *correctness* signal $`q_{t}`$ is dropped: the
resulting executed action is no longer scored for syntactic validity,
semantic appropriateness, or domain consistency. The drop of $`-12.1`$
points reflects that without local correctness, the policy retains
interventions that were locally invalid (e.g. a malformed SEARCH
argument) as long as the trajectory eventually succeeded.

w/o Outcome. The *outcome* signal $`o_{t}`$ is dropped: the per-step
score no longer ties intervention quality to downstream EM, cost, or
side-effects. The drop of $`-12.8`$ points reflects that without outcome
credit, the model can over-internalize PF-aligned trajectories that look
right locally but do not improve final answers.

The four drops together support the framework’s central claim that
PF-derived supervision is irreducible to a single scalar: each of
*when*, *how*, *whether well-formed*, and *whether it paid off*
contributes a distinct $`7`$–$`15`$ points to the closed-loop run.

### G.3 Filtering Ablation

The third block of
Table [5](#S4.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 4.1 Main Results: PF Intervention, Selection, and Internalization ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ Harnessing LLM Agents with Skill Programs")
evaluates the effect of admission control during library evolution. All
rows use the same E5 closed-loop rejection sampling configuration with
all four signals active; the only knob that varies is which of
executable validation (Exec) and teacher review (Teach) gates a
candidate skill before it is appended to the library
(§[C.4](#A3.SS4 "C.4 Phase D — Executable Validation ‣ Appendix C Self-Improving Pipeline Details ‣ Harnessing LLM Agents with Skill Programs")–[C.6](#A3.SS6 "C.6 Phase F — Library Update and Versioning ‣ Appendix C Self-Improving Pipeline Details ‣ Harnessing LLM Agents with Skill Programs")).

Evolution, full filtering. Both Exec and Teach are required: a candidate
must pass the four executable checks of
§[C.4](#A3.SS4 "C.4 Phase D — Executable Validation ‣ Appendix C Self-Improving Pipeline Details ‣ Harnessing LLM Agents with Skill Programs")
*and* reach $`Q_{\mathrm{skill}}\geq 0.60`$ on the five-dimensional
teacher review of
§[C.5](#A3.SS5 "C.5 Phase E — Teacher Five-Dimensional Review ‣ Appendix C Self-Improving Pipeline Details ‣ Harnessing LLM Agents with Skill Programs").
Reference row at $`60.3\%`$.

No evolution. Library evolution is turned off entirely; the run is
otherwise identical to E5, but the library remains the seed snapshot
throughout training. This is effectively the V1 RS analogue (E2)
measured under the same protocol. At $`59.3\%`$, only $`-1.0`$ point
below full evolution, this row shows that closed-loop evolution is a
genuine but modest contributor on top of a strong fixed library.

Evolution, no filtering. Evolution is turned on but *neither* Exec nor
Teach is enforced — every candidate proposed in Phase C is appended to
the library without any gate. The drop of $`-24.0`$ points is the
central evidence for the memory-pollution hypothesis: unfiltered
candidates include skills that fail to import, skills that fire too
aggressively, and skills that conflict with existing PFs, and the
resulting noise in the retrieval pool degrades downstream policy
decisions even when the rollout configuration is otherwise unchanged.
This row is also the only one in the panel that falls *below* the
multi-loop baseline of the first block ($`36.3`$ vs. $`31.2`$), showing
that bad library evolution can be actively harmful rather than merely
useless.

Evolution, exec-only. Only the executable validation gate of
§[C.4](#A3.SS4 "C.4 Phase D — Executable Validation ‣ Appendix C Self-Improving Pipeline Details ‣ Harnessing LLM Agents with Skill Programs")
is applied; teacher review is skipped, so syntactically valid but
conceptually weak or overly specific candidates are admitted. The drop
of $`-11.5`$ points indicates that the executable gate alone catches the
catastrophic interface failures (which is why this row is far above “no
filtering”) but is not enough to keep retrieval precision high, because
the library accumulates plausible-looking but uninformative skills.

Evolution, teacher-only. Only the teacher review gate of
§[C.5](#A3.SS5 "C.5 Phase E — Teacher Five-Dimensional Review ‣ Appendix C Self-Improving Pipeline Details ‣ Harnessing LLM Agents with Skill Programs")
is applied; the four executable checks are skipped, so candidates that
the teacher rates highly on concept but cannot actually run end up in
the library. The drop of $`-13.1`$ points shows that the teacher’s
conceptual judgments are insufficient on their own: a candidate with a
well-articulated concept but a malformed intervene method still emits
runtime errors that disable the surrounding skill at inference, and the
resulting interface inconsistency erodes the gains from healthy skills.

Together, the four non-default rows trace a clean ordering: full
filtering ($`60.3`$) $`>`$ no evolution ($`59.3`$) $`>`$ exec-only
($`48.8`$) $`>`$ teacher-only ($`47.2`$) $`>`$ no filtering ($`36.3`$).
Both gates are necessary: executable validation prevents broken or
ill-typed skills, teacher review filters conceptually weak ones, and
removing either gate falls back to a regime where the noise added by
evolution outweighs the benefit of new skills. The pattern justifies our
policy of treating self-improving PF evolution as a *validated and
rate-limited* process rather than unconstrained skill generation.

Figure 5: Optimization diagnostics for the six post-training settings.
Left: gradient norm as a function of processed training tokens. Right:
learning rate as a function of processed training tokens. These curves
help distinguish genuine differences in training dynamics from artifacts
of optimization instability or scheduler choice, and provide additional
context for the phase transitions observed in the main training plots.

Figure 6: Training dynamics of all six post-training settings plotted
against global step. From left to right, we report training loss,
correction-aligned token accuracy, and policy entropy. This figure
complements
Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.1 Main Results: PF Intervention, Selection, and Internalization ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ Harnessing LLM Agents with Skill Programs")
by showing that the qualitative differences across recipes remain
visible under a step-based view rather than only under token
normalization.

Figure 7: Open-loop training dynamics under a fixed PF library. We
compare supervised fine-tuning, rejection sampling, and on-policy
distillation in terms of training loss, correction-aligned token
accuracy, and policy entropy as functions of processed training tokens.
By removing closed-loop evolution from the comparison, this figure
isolates how the three post-training recipes differ when trained on the
same fixed PF-aware rollout pool.

Figure 8: Closed-loop training dynamics under evolving PF libraries. We
compare supervised fine-tuning, rejection sampling, and on-policy
distillation in terms of training loss, correction-aligned token
accuracy, and policy entropy as functions of processed training tokens.
The vertical dotted marker indicates the first refresh point of the
closed-loop pipeline. This figure highlights how evolving PF supervision
changes the optimization trajectory relative to the fixed-library
setting.

### G.4 Case Study

To complement the aggregated recovery statistics in
Table [16](#A7.T16 "Table 16 ‣ G.4 Case Study ‣ Appendix G Signal and Filtering Ablations ‣ Harnessing LLM Agents with Skill Programs"),
this section walks through one concrete trajectory per domain in which
the baseline (RA-Agent multi-loop) fails and our PF-augmented agent
succeeds. For each case we render the *full* ReAct rollout: at every
step we show the agent’s internal *thought*, the proposed action, the
observation returned, and (for our agent) every PF activation event with
its trigger, intervention type, and the before/after action or context.
The intent is to make the corrective mechanism visible in the policy
loop, not just in the aggregated statistics. All cases use
Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with the rollout configuration of
§[D](#A4 "Appendix D Additional Experimental Details ‣ Harnessing LLM Agents with Skill Programs");
the trajectories are taken verbatim from the evaluation logs.

|                            |                      |              |
|----------------------------|----------------------|--------------|
| Failure Type               | Corrective Mechanism | Coverage (%) |
| entity_conf                | resolved_entity      | 37–43        |
| retrieval + insuff_explore | better_search        | 29–33        |
| reasoning                  | corrected_reasoning  | 15           |
| read_comp                  | deeper_reading       | 8–9          |
| format                     | improved_format      | 5            |
| hallucination              | —                    | $`{<}1`$     |

Table 16: Recovered failure cases and their corresponding corrective
mechanisms. Percentages are computed over recovered cases only. The
largest gains come from resolving entity confusion and improving search
under insufficient exploration, followed by corrected reasoning and
deeper reading.

#### Web-search case: HotpotQA — multi-hop entity resolution

The question is a three-hop query (*Walton family member* $`\to`$ *died
after John in 2005* $`\to`$ *her husband*). Both agents use the same
SEARCH/READ/FINAL action space and the same teacher-augmented retriever,
but only our agent decomposes the query, forces a READ before FINAL, and
verifies completeness.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Phase-by-phase comparison. The baseline’s three steps reproduce the
canonical multi-step failure modes targeted by Phase B
(§[C.2](#A3.SS2 "C.2 Phase B — Failure Signal Detection ‣ Appendix C Self-Improving Pipeline Details ‣ Harnessing LLM Agents with Skill Programs")):
no_read_before_final (it never READs), repeated_search (steps 1 and 2
issue identical queries), and reasoning_hallucination at FINAL (the
answer “Bruce Walton” is not present in any retrieved snippet). Our
agent triggers three PFs at three distinct loop locations: (i) *before*
step 0’s SEARCH, decompose_complex_question fires as an INJECT_CONTEXT
that surfaces a decomposition hint into the next observation, steering
the agent toward hop-by-hop search; (ii) *at* step 2, the agent’s
proposed action is FINAL with no prior READ, so insufficient_exploration
fires as a MODIFY_ACTION that overrides the action from FINAL("Sam
Walton") to READ(doc_0) — the explicit before/after pair is
(action=FINAL,arg="Sam Walton") $`\to`$ (action=READ,arg="doc_0"); (iii)
*at* step 3, after the agent emits a single-token FINAL("Sam"),
answer_completeness fires as an INJECT_CONTEXT reminding the policy that
the question has multiple parts, prompting the model to expand to the
gold-standard form "Sam Walton". Each intervention has an inspectable
trigger, an explicit before-action / after-action pair, and a logged
reason — the trajectory itself is the audit trail. None of these three
corrections is a stronger model: PFs intervene on the *same* Qwen-7B
policy that produced the baseline.

#### Math case: AMC23 — distinct-roots polynomial counting

For math, the rollout is single-step (max_steps $`=1`$,
§[B.4](#A2.SS4 "B.4 Skill Libraries Across Domains ‣ Appendix B Additional Details of HASP Framework ‣ Harnessing LLM Agents with Skill Programs")),
so the entire ReAct loop is one \<think\>/FINAL pair. Skills enter
through (a) system_summary prompts injected into the system message
during PFSelector stage, and (b) a pre_final verifier hook on the FINAL
action. Both agents see the same problem; the only difference is whether
the math skill library is active.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Phase-by-phase comparison. Both agents share the same Vieta setup; the
difference is structural rather than mathematical. The baseline’s
failure is captured exactly by the heuristic detector
case_incompleteness of
§[C.2](#A3.SS2 "C.2 Phase B — Failure Signal Detection ‣ Appendix C Self-Improving Pipeline Details ‣ Harnessing LLM Agents with Skill Programs"):
it lists nine *orderings* but the question counts *ordered $`(a,b)`$
pairs*, and Vieta’s symmetric polynomials collapse permutations of the
same root multiset onto the same $`(a,b)`$. Two PFs intervene through
different surfaces: case_incompleteness and overgeneralization fire
jointly as a pre_final phase instruction (an INJECT_CONTEXT-style
intervention) that surfaces a constraint reminder *before* the model
commits its count; verification_missing (priority $`0.90`$, always-on)
fires as a pre_final verification hook that forces a substitution check
on each candidate $`(a,b)`$. The before/after for the agent’s draft is
(count = 9 over orderings) $`\to`$ (count = 5 over consolidated
multisets, each substitution-verified). As in the search case, no
stronger model is invoked — the same Qwen-7B policy is steered onto a
self-consistent counting frame.

#### Coding case: LiveCodeBench-easy — “Equally”

Coding rollouts use max_steps $`=1`$ as well; PFs run as static-analysis
hooks on the emitted code body and emit INJECT_CONTEXT hints rather than
rewriting code. The visible repair is the agent’s revised solution after
the static check fires.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Phase-by-phase comparison. The baseline’s solution misses one branch of
the case analysis: when $`A=B=C`$, the partition into three singleton
groups always works, but its disjunction a+b==c or a+c==b or b+c==a only
covers two-vs-one partitions. The corresponding heuristic in Phase B is
partial_answer / case_incompleteness, and the runtime PF code_edge_cases
catches it through a static check on the FINAL code body (branching
disjunction without an all-equal short-circuit) and injects a context
hint that explicitly walks (2,2,2) through the branches. The
intervention type is INJECT_CONTEXT, not MODIFY_ACTION — the framework
does not rewrite the student’s code; the policy itself adds the a == b
== c branch in response to the hint. The before/after pair is (branches:
{odd, zero, two-of-three}) $`\to`$ (branches: {all-equal, odd,
sum$`\leq 3`$, sum$`\in\{4,6\}`$, two-of-three, else}), with the only
structural change being the all-equal branch added at the top.

## Appendix H Training Dynamics

This section unpacks the training-dynamics figures, makes the
data-collection protocol explicit, and reads each curve back to a
property of the recipe rather than treating the plots as decoration. All
six runs use the same Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct LoRA fine-tuning configuration
of
§[D](#A4 "Appendix D Additional Experimental Details ‣ Harnessing LLM Agents with Skill Programs")
(rank $`16`$, $`\alpha=32`$, bf16, gradient checkpointing; the
recipe-specific knobs (learning rate, number of epochs, rollout shape)
are summarized in
Table [13](#A4.T13 "Table 13 ‣ D.3 Shared Training Configuration ‣ Appendix D Additional Experimental Details ‣ Harnessing LLM Agents with Skill Programs").

### H.1 Data-Collection Protocol

The curves in
Figures [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.1 Main Results: PF Intervention, Selection, and Internalization ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ Harnessing LLM Agents with Skill Programs")
and
[5](#A7.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ G.3 Filtering Ablation ‣ Appendix G Signal and Filtering Ablations ‣ Harnessing LLM Agents with Skill Programs")–[8](#A7.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ G.3 Filtering Ablation ‣ Appendix G Signal and Filtering Ablations ‣ Harnessing LLM Agents with Skill Programs")
are produced from Weights & Biases run logs. The trainer (TRL’s
SFTTrainer for E1/E4 and the rejection-sampling/distillation drivers for
E2/E3/E5/E6) emits one JSON-style loss-dict per logging interval
(logging_steps $`=10`$) into output.log. Each emitted dict reports the
seven scalars we plot: loss, grad_norm, learning_rate, entropy,
num_tokens, mean_token_accuracy, and epoch. The three primary signals in
the main-text figure correspond to (i) cross-entropy training loss, (ii)
per-step *correction-aligned token accuracy* (the trainer’s
mean_token_accuracy, computed over the PF-corrected target tokens,
$`\tilde{a}_{t}`$, rather than the raw policy outputs), and (iii)
on-policy generation entropy as estimated by TRL during the forward
pass. Curves are smoothed with a centered moving-average window of size
$`5`$ to suppress per-step noise without distorting the slow-time-scale
shape.

For each E we plot one canonical run — the longest single Wandb run
available for V1, and the concatenation of iter_0 and iter_1 for the
closed-loop V2 settings (the smallest sequence that captures the first
evolution boundary). Concretely the canonical traces are: E1 V1 SFT for
$`600`$ optimizer steps over $`\approx 10`$ epochs; E2 V1 RS for
$`1{,}400`$ optimizer steps over $`8`$ epochs $`\times`$ $`2`$ RS
iterations; E3 V1 OPD for $`900`$ optimizer steps over $`10`$ epochs; E4
V2 SFT as $`820`$ + $`180`$ steps across two closed-loop iterations; E5
V2 RS as $`700`$ + $`360`$ steps; and E6 V2 OPD as $`280`$ + $`140`$
steps. Token counts (num_tokens) are accumulated across iterations so
the V2 X-axes remain monotone; the iter-boundary in each V2 series is
rendered as a vertical dotted marker in the run’s own color.

### H.2 Optimization Diagnostics

Figure [5](#A7.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ G.3 Filtering Ablation ‣ Appendix G Signal and Filtering Ablations ‣ Harnessing LLM Agents with Skill Programs")
reports gradient norm and learning rate against processed tokens. The
gradient-norm panel verifies that the loss differences across recipes
are not artifacts of unstable optimization: all six runs sit in the same
magnitude band ($`\sim 10^{0}`$ to $`10^{1}`$) with no run-specific
spikes at the iter-boundaries, ruling out the hypothesis that the small
loss bumps in V2 reflect numerical issues. The learning-rate panel makes
the schedule explicit: SFT uses $`1\times 10^{-5}`$ peak (E1, E4); RS
and OPD use $`5\times 10^{-6}`$ (E2, E3, E5, E6) because they operate on
top of an SFT-warmed policy; warmup is $`3\%`$ of total tokens for all
six. Closed-loop runs apply the schedule per iter rather than globally,
so each V2 curve shows a fresh warmup at the iter-boundary — the
iter-internal LR pattern is repeated, not flattened. Reading the
optimization panel together with the loss panel makes clear that the
recipe-level differences in convergence rate and final level reflect the
objective rather than the optimizer.

### H.3 Loop-Topology Comparisons

Three companion figures separate the data along orthogonal axes.
Figure [6](#A7.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ G.3 Filtering Ablation ‣ Appendix G Signal and Filtering Ablations ‣ Harnessing LLM Agents with Skill Programs")
replots all six runs against *global step* rather than tokens to confirm
that recipe ordering is robust to X-axis choice: V2 runs span fewer
steps but more wall-clock seconds because the evolve cycle inserts
inference and skill-proposal stages between training phases.
Figures [7](#A7.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ G.3 Filtering Ablation ‣ Appendix G Signal and Filtering Ablations ‣ Harnessing LLM Agents with Skill Programs")
and
[8](#A7.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ G.3 Filtering Ablation ‣ Appendix G Signal and Filtering Ablations ‣ Harnessing LLM Agents with Skill Programs")
each show only three curves — the V1-only and V2-only subsets
respectively — which makes the recipe-vs-recipe contrast easier to see
without cross-topology visual clutter. The vertical dotted marker in
Figure [8](#A7.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ G.3 Filtering Ablation ‣ Appendix G Signal and Filtering Ablations ‣ Harnessing LLM Agents with Skill Programs")
marks the first closed-loop refresh point in each V2 run. The most
informative comparison is V1 SFT
(Figure [7](#A7.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ G.3 Filtering Ablation ‣ Appendix G Signal and Filtering Ablations ‣ Harnessing LLM Agents with Skill Programs"))
versus V2 SFT
(Figure [8](#A7.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ G.3 Filtering Ablation ‣ Appendix G Signal and Filtering Ablations ‣ Harnessing LLM Agents with Skill Programs")):
the V1 curve is smooth, the V2 curve shows a cleanly visible break at
the iter-boundary, and after the break the slope flattens because the
post-evolve target pool has higher accuracy targets to reach. This is
direct evidence that the closed-loop refresh changes the gradient signal
rather than merely re-running the same data.

trigger is the consistently lowest-scoring dimension
($`0.65`$–$`0.87`$), echoing the recurring difficulty of writing a
should_activate predicate that is neither too broad nor too narrow — the

(Listing [C.5](#A3.SS5 "C.5 Phase E — Teacher Five-Dimensional Review ‣ Appendix C Self-Improving Pipeline Details ‣ Harnessing LLM Agents with Skill Programs")).

three domains: reasoning_hallucination
($`Q_{\mathrm{skill}}=0.89`$/$`0.90`$/$`0.91`$ on web/math/code) and
premature_final ($`0.88`$/$`0.89`$/$`0.86`$). These are also the two
families that contribute the largest validation uplift
(reasoning_hallucination: $`+9.3`$ avg. points on web;
Table [17](#A9.T17 "Table 17 ‣ Appendix I Additional Analysis of Skill Evolution ‣ Harnessing LLM Agents with Skill Programs")),
so high review scores correlate with downstream utility rather than
being free credit.

### I.2 Per-Domain Filter Outcomes and Admission Counts

Table [19](#A9.T19 "Table 19 ‣ I.2 Per-Domain Filter Outcomes and Admission Counts ‣ Appendix I Additional Analysis of Skill Evolution ‣ Harnessing LLM Agents with Skill Programs")
reports library-growth statistics across the three domains. The
closed-loop runs span $`5`$ epochs for web-search and $`3`$ epochs each
for math and code under the lite-evolve schedule of
§[D.5](#A4.SS5 "D.5 Closed-Loop Evolution Modes ‣ Appendix D Additional Experimental Details ‣ Harnessing LLM Agents with Skill Programs");
the proposer is rate-limited to at most five candidates per epoch
(max_candidates_per_epoch,
§[C.3](#A3.SS3 "C.3 Phase C — Skill Proposal ‣ Appendix C Self-Improving Pipeline Details ‣ Harnessing LLM Agents with Skill Programs")),
and the library is hard-capped at max_library_size $`=50`$ active
skills. Under the current “audit-only” acceptance policy of
§[C.4](#A3.SS4 "C.4 Phase D — Executable Validation ‣ Appendix C Self-Improving Pipeline Details ‣ Harnessing LLM Agents with Skill Programs")–[C.5](#A3.SS5 "C.5 Phase E — Teacher Five-Dimensional Review ‣ Appendix C Self-Improving Pipeline Details ‣ Harnessing LLM Agents with Skill Programs"),
all candidates that compile are appended to the library with their
review scores stored alongside, so that closed-loop policies can flip
the gate on without re-running rollouts.

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Domain | Epochs | Accepted | Distinct families | Mean $`Q_{\mathrm{skill}}`$ | Min | Max |
| Web-search | $`5`$ | $`18`$ | $`5`$ | $`0.85`$ | $`0.745`$ | $`0.965`$ |
| Math | $`3`$ | $`12`$ | $`4`$ | $`0.83`$ | $`0.740`$ | $`0.925`$ |
| Code | $`3`$ | $`55`$ | $`8`$ | $`0.80`$ | $`0.665`$ | $`0.965`$ |

Table 19: Library growth statistics across self-improvement rounds, by
domain. “Mean $`Q_{\mathrm{skill}}`$” averages over accepted candidates;
“Min” and “Max” report extremes. Under the strict
$`Q_{\mathrm{skill}}\geq 0.60`$ acceptance threshold of
§[C.5](#A3.SS5 "C.5 Phase E — Teacher Five-Dimensional Review ‣ Appendix C Self-Improving Pipeline Details ‣ Harnessing LLM Agents with Skill Programs"),
every accepted candidate would still be admitted
($`\min Q_{\mathrm{skill}}\geq 0.665`$ across all three domains).

The web-search and math runs admit between $`4`$ and $`6`$ candidates
per epoch, comfortably under the per-epoch cap; the code run admits more
candidates per epoch ($`\sim 18`$) because its lite-evolve schedule
(§[D.5](#A4.SS5 "D.5 Closed-Loop Evolution Modes ‣ Appendix D Additional Experimental Details ‣ Harnessing LLM Agents with Skill Programs"))
re-samples failed trajectories more aggressively and the proposer emits
multiple variants per residual cluster. Even with this faster growth,
the active library never exceeds the $`50`$-skill hard cap, because each
admission goes into a versioned slot (\_\_v{N}) and only the latest
version of each base id (skill_ids_latest) is exposed at runtime. Older
versions remain on disk for trajectory replay but never fire, so
retrieval precision is bounded by the number of distinct skill families
($`5`$/$`4`$/$`8`$ across web/math/code) rather than the cumulative
count of accepted versions.

### I.3 Filtering Outcomes Under the Strict-Gate Policy

Although the current pipeline is in audit-only mode, the on-disk scores
let us reconstruct what the strict-gate policy of
§[C.5](#A3.SS5 "C.5 Phase E — Teacher Five-Dimensional Review ‣ Appendix C Self-Improving Pipeline Details ‣ Harnessing LLM Agents with Skill Programs")
would do. With $`Q_{\mathrm{exec}}\geq 0.30`$ for hard rejection,
$`Q_{\mathrm{skill}}\geq 0.60`$ for acceptance, and
$`Q_{\mathrm{skill}}\geq 0.75`$ for new-category admission, all $`85`$
candidates accepted across the three domains would still pass the basic
acceptance threshold ($`\min Q_{\mathrm{skill}}=0.665`$ in code), but
only $`52`$ of $`85`$ ($`61\%`$) would clear the new-category bar of
$`0.75`$. The boundary cases concentrate in the families with the lowest
review scores — format_mismatch (math/code), wrong_entity_focus (code),
incomplete_logic, and incomplete_implementation (code) — which in our
system are generally accepted as refinements of an existing seed family
rather than new categories. This is consistent with the multi-tier
threshold design: the framework lets a weak refinement past the
same-family bar while reserving the higher bar for genuinely new skill
concepts. The same-family bar is what controls library noise during
rapid evolution, and it is the lever that the filtering ablation in
Table [5](#S4.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 4.1 Main Results: PF Intervention, Selection, and Internalization ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ Harnessing LLM Agents with Skill Programs")
exercises directly.

### I.4 Skill-Family Evolution Pattern

Across all three domains the evolved library converges on a small set of
recurring families that map onto the Phase B failure-detector taxonomy
(§[C.2](#A3.SS2 "C.2 Phase B — Failure Signal Detection ‣ Appendix C Self-Improving Pipeline Details ‣ Harnessing LLM Agents with Skill Programs")):
premature_final, no_read_before_final, reasoning_hallucination,
wrong_entity_focus, and format_mismatch dominate the web-search and math
libraries, and the same five plus
incomplete_implementation/incomplete_logic dominate code. This
convergence is informative: the proposer (the student vLLM) is choosing
skill ids that overlap heavily with the heuristic detectors of Phase B
even though it sees the failure clusters as natural-language
abstractions, not as named heuristics. In other words, the student
rediscovers the failure taxonomy from data rather than copying it from
labels — which we read as a sanity check that the closed-loop signal is
not collapsing to the proposer reproducing a fixed list. The
cross-domain reuse of family names also explains why the lite-evolve
mode is sufficient for E5/E6: most epochs add a refinement of an
already-named family rather than a genuinely new concept, and the
executable validation pipeline
(§[C.4](#A3.SS4 "C.4 Phase D — Executable Validation ‣ Appendix C Self-Improving Pipeline Details ‣ Harnessing LLM Agents with Skill Programs"))
is what keeps refinements compatible with the existing dispatcher.

### J.3 Teacher API Budget

All teacher-augmented stages call gpt-4o (snapshot gpt-4o-2024-11-20)
through the standard OpenAI Chat Completions API. We pinned this
snapshot for all experiments to keep the teacher behavior reproducible
across the paper’s lifetime; any future change to OpenAI’s default
gpt-4o alias would not affect the reported numbers but *would* affect
re-runs unless the snapshot suffix is preserved. Approximate token
counts per stage, aggregated across the full paper, are: $`\sim 80`$ M
input + $`10`$ M output for skill-eval inference (across all eight
ablation rows), $`\sim 25`$ M input + $`5`$ M output for the three
self-improving loops (Phase A–H total), and $`\sim 20`$ M input +
$`4`$ M output for the on-policy distillation runs (E3, E6). The single
most expensive stage is full evolve in E4 ($`\sim 1`$ h per evolve
cycle, two cycles), driven by the Phase E teacher review of every
candidate. Lite evolve in E5/E6 makes *no* teacher API calls.

### J.4 Random Seeds and Variance

All training runs use seed $`=42`$ (Hugging Face TrainingArguments.seed
and Python random.seed) for the trainer, and a separate fixed seed for
the validation-pool shuffle in
§[D.1](#A4.SS1 "D.1 Datasets and Train/Test Splits ‣ Appendix D Additional Experimental Details ‣ Harnessing LLM Agents with Skill Programs").
Rollout sampling under RS and OPD uses temperature $`0.9`$ / top-$`p`$
$`0.95`$, so trajectory generation is non-deterministic; the variance
across re-rollouts is bounded primarily by group size $`g=2`$ rather
than by seed choice. We report all results from a single seed because
re-running E1–E6 across multiple seeds is prohibitive
($`\approx 6\times`$ the compute budget); based on internal smoke tests
with $`g=4`$ rollouts, the standard deviation of the web-search EM
average is approximately $`\pm 1.5`$ points across re-runs of the same
seed, which is smaller than the gaps reported in
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.1 Main Results: PF Intervention, Selection, and Internalization ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ Harnessing LLM Agents with Skill Programs").
We flag the absence of multi-seed numbers as a known limitation.

### J.5 Software, Code, and Checkpoint Release

The codebase is implemented in Python (3.11) on top of transformers,
trl, peft, and vllm; exact pinned versions are recorded in the
repository’s requirements.txt. The skill library, generated PFs,
library-history JSONs, and training-data jsonls live under
self_improving/; the PF runtime is in src/skills_agent/skills/.
Pre-trained LoRA adapters for E1–E6 and the evolved skill libraries will
be released with the camera-ready under a permissive license; teacher
API logs are not released because they contain raw third-party API
responses, but the prompts that produce them are fully documented in
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Self-Improving Pipeline Details ‣ Harnessing LLM Agents with Skill Programs")
(Boxes [C.2](#A3.SS2 "C.2 Phase B — Failure Signal Detection ‣ Appendix C Self-Improving Pipeline Details ‣ Harnessing LLM Agents with Skill Programs")–[C.5](#A3.SS5 "C.5 Phase E — Teacher Five-Dimensional Review ‣ Appendix C Self-Improving Pipeline Details ‣ Harnessing LLM Agents with Skill Programs")).
The full validation/test split files generated under
self_improving/data/ are deterministic given the source
AgentFlow-aligned datasets, the seed boundary in
Table [10](#A4.T10 "Table 10 ‣ D.1 Datasets and Train/Test Splits ‣ Appendix D Additional Experimental Details ‣ Harnessing LLM Agents with Skill Programs"),
and seed $`=42`$; we will release these as well to remove ambiguity.

## Appendix K Cost and Latency Breakdown

The framework instantiates a teacher model at up to $`17`$ distinct
invocation sites per episode
(§[B.6](#A2.SS6 "B.6 Multi-Layer Skill Selection at Inference ‣ Appendix B Additional Details of HASP Framework ‣ Harnessing LLM Agents with Skill Programs")).
This section quantifies the per-episode token budget and approximate
dollar cost of each setting in
Table [5](#S4.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 4.1 Main Results: PF Intervention, Selection, and Internalization ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ Harnessing LLM Agents with Skill Programs"),
so that practical adoption decisions can be made without recomputing the
budget from first principles. All numbers refer to the web-search domain
(which has the longest rollouts); math and code costs are roughly
$`30`$–$`50\%`$ lower because rollouts collapse to a single step.

### K.1 Per-Setting Cost Aggregates

We estimate token cost using the OpenAI gpt-4o-2024-11-20 list price at
the time of the experiments (input \$$`2.50`$/M, output \$$`10.00`$/M).
Under the full HASP setting, the average cost is approximately
\$$`0.045`$ per question. We also report wall-clock time per episode
(median over $`200`$ samples), so readers can translate these costs into
approximate API throughput if needed.

The main cost comes from the eight FINAL-time LLM-assisted handlers
(§[B.6](#A2.SS6 "B.6 Multi-Layer Skill Selection at Inference ‣ Appendix B Additional Details of HASP Framework ‣ Harnessing LLM Agents with Skill Programs")),
which together account for about 50% of teacher tokens per episode in
the full setting. Mid-rollout PFs (retrieval_failure,
format_extraction_error, reasoning_error, and answer_confidence_guard)
are rate-limited and contribute about 10%. Pre-rollout components such
as the Difficulty Gate and PFSelector cost about 2k tokens once per
episode, so their relative cost becomes smaller on longer multi-step
rollouts. Format post-processing is consistently about 0.5k tokens per
FINAL action.
````
